newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Sneeze-injured British climber vows to try again.
newsitem.headline: Sneeze-injured British climber vows to try again.

text.p: A British climber whose attempt to conquer the 14 highest peaks in the world was foiled by a sneeze last week vowed on Monday to return to Pakistan next year to complete his mission.
"In next June, I will come back to do Nanga Parbat," Alan Hinkes told reporters, lying sideways on a grassy lawn of a private hospital treating him for a slipped disc.

Hinkes was earlier airlifted from the base camp of the 8,126-metre (26,660-foot) high Nanga Parbat, in northern Pakistan, locally known as the "killer mountain" for the many deaths of climbers on its slopes.
"I will definitely come back next year," he said.

Hinkes, from northern England, pulled a muscle in his back while eating the thin unleavened local bread called "chapati" on the mountainside. Flour on the chapati blew into his face, causing him to sneeze.
"It is pretty embarrassing because it was a humble chapati," Hinkes said.
"The sneeze was caused by a bit of flour up my nose and I sneezed and completely spasmed, badly, and seemed like I slipped a disc actually."

Hinkes had already climbed nine of the 14 "8,000" peaks, so called because they rise above 8,000 metres (26,000 feet), and was attempting a world first by climbing the remaining five in the space of 12 months.
"I was 13,000 feet (4,000 metres) in the high base camp area, about three or four days from the road head," he recalled. "I couldn't walk for the first three days, couldn't even crawl.
"Yesterday I managed to stagger down to 11,000 feet (3,350 metres) or a bit lower using ski sticks to stagger down."
Adding to his woes, a helicopter which was supposed to airlift him from the base camp first went to the wrong valley and later encountered weather and refuelling problems.
"It was just one of those things, like the chapati incident. Just bad luck," he said.
"They went into the wrong valley to start with, then the weather got bad and then they had to reposition for fuel."
Hinkes' accomplishments include scaling the 8,847-metre (29,028-foot) Mount Everest, the world's highest peak, and the 8,610-metre (28,250-foot) K-2, the second highest, in 1995 and 1996.

He said he was undeterred by this latest setback, adding that he had had a "stupid accident" before when he fell off a path while trekking in Nepal and in 1992 was once caught in a major rock avalanche for 15 seconds on a steep ice face.
"I am bit off chapatis at the moment I must say, because that was all the food that was left...," he said of the latest incident. "I am sick of the smell of chapatis."
Hinkes said he hoped to return home next week after a five-day treatment of ultra-sound and some exercises.
Earlier on Monday, Hinkes faxed a statement to his sponsors in Britain, saying: "It's amazing that something as trivial as eating a chapati could have landed me in such trouble."
